newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada sent wrong message to China - HK activist.
newsitem.headline: Canada sent wrong message to China - HK activist.

text.p: Canada sent the wrong message to China this week when it did not support a U.N. resolution criticizing Beijing's human rights record, Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigner Martin Lee said on Thursday.

"It gives the world, including China, the wrong message, that Canada seems to be in doubt about her commitment to support of democracy and human rights for the rest of the world," Lee said before meeting Prime Minister Jean Chretien.

Lee, who is scheduled to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday, is on an international tour to bolster support for Hong Kong's democracy movement before Hong Kong, a British colony, reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.

Canada, which has actively sought to boost trade with China, withdrew its usual co-sponsorship for an annual resolution on China in the U.N. Human Rights Commission, saying bilateral committees and visits would be more effective.
Chretien, asked by reporters on Thursday to explain the decision, said one reason was that China had not used its U.N. Security Council veto in a case of interest to Canada.

"Because we have established good relations with them, they withdrew in June last year their veto so that we could keep Canadian (peacekeeping) troops...under the umbrella of the U.N. in Haiti," he said. "So in politics you have to make difficult decisions."
China had threatened to veto the military force, which Canada now commands, because of Haiti's diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Chretien, speaking before meeting Lee, said another reason was that the European Union had broken ranks on what had been a Western consensus.
"France, the Germans, the Italians, the Spaniards and others quit... So we looked at what was for us the best solution, and the best solution is to engage (China)," he said.
Lee, chairman of the Hong Kong Democratic Party, said China needed trade and it was wrong to think trade would suffer if countries stuck to principles on human rights.

"I think what is important is if you make your position known to the Chinese leaders first and say, 'Now this is our policy whether you like it or not. We would of course like to have good relations with you and more trade with you but we cannot depart and we will not depart from our policy'," he said.
"Once they know that and you really stick to it they respect you for it."

Lee said Canada and the United States had a moral obligation to tell China it must adhere to promises made to Hong Kong because in 1984 China sought their support for the Sino-British pact under which the colony will return to Chinese rule.
"That is my principal message -- to keep at least Hong Kong free when it is returned to the motherland," he said.
China's top policy official on Hong Kong, Lu Ping, began a tour of Canada in Vancouver on Wednesday to promote Beijing's views on Hong Kong.
In a brief session with reporters, he dismissed the meeting between Lee and Chretien as insignificant.
